paragraph.text: consideration for animals doesn't depend on utilitarianism. Equal consideration is a formal principle: it says we shouldn't be biased when weighing each individual's interests, whatever theory we use to decide what to do. Utilitarians, rights theorists, contractualists, egalitarians and capabilities theorists disagree about almost everything, and even so they have arrived at the rejection of speciesism. Knocking down utilitarianism doesn't rescue animal exploitation.
"All this animal rights talk comes from Peter Singer, who's a utilitarian. And utilitarianism justifies horrible things."
The main argument for considering animals comes from Peter Singer's utilitarianism.
Utilitarianism has unacceptable consequences, such as allowing an innocent person to be sacrificed to benefit many.
A conclusion that depends on a false theory isn't justified.
So the case for considering animals isn't justified.
P2 has the support of many philosophers, and it's true that Singer's
fails at P1: consideration for animals is defended by theories that reject utilitarianism.
"The sentience criterion only makes sense in a utilitarian ethics."

Imagine three teachers who disagree about how to share a cake: one wants to give more to whoever is hungriest, another wants equal slices, another wants to draw lots. But all three agree you can't leave a child without cake just because they have red hair. It's similar with animals: people who study ethics disagree about many things, but many agree it isn't fair to let someone suffer just because they belong to another species.

It isn't. Tom Regan defended animal rights and was a harsh critic of utilitarianism. Martha Nussbaum starts from the capabilities approach. Mark Rowlands uses contractualism, and there are defenses from virtue and care ethics, among others. Each theory takes a different path, but they all reach a common point: animals count, and species alone doesn't justify ignoring their interests. In 2022, more than 500 philosophers from different traditions signed the Montreal Declaration, which condemns animal exploitation. Those who consider utilitarianism wrong can debate it, and also learn how other moral and political views show that speciesism is still left without a justification.
"Which ethical theory do you think is correct? Let's see what it says about making animals suffer without need."
Who counts and how to weigh without bias
Equal consideration is compatible with any theory that isn't biased. Utilitarianism is only one of them.

The rejection of speciesism has been defended by rights theories (Regan), contractualist ones (Rowlands), the capabilities approach (Nussbaum), virtue and care ethics, among others, each with its own reasoning:
For Regan, every "subject-of-a-life" has inherent value and may not be treated as a mere means, human or not.
(2023), Nussbaum rejects both utilitarianism and the Kantian view and argues that every sentient creature should have the opportunity to flourish in the form of life characteristic of its kind.

Rowlands proposes that, behind Rawls's "veil of ignorance", those choosing principles don't know whether they'll be human or another animal, and so would choose principles that protect animals. This reading is contested: other contractualists, such as Peter Carruthers, conclude that animals have no direct moral standing, and some argue Rowlands's version departs from Rawls.
See the overview in "The state of the art in animal ethics", in the Beyond veganism section.

text.bold: 2. Rival theories agree on the conclusion.

paragraph.text: Imagine two rescued animals and two ways of sheltering them. The utilitarian picks the one that maximizes the total good, the maximin supporter picks the one that improves the situation of whoever is worst off, the egalitarian picks the one that reduces inequality. All of them keep the same decision if the individuals swap places. Whoever changes the decision only because of species is no longer following any of these theories.

text.bold: 3. Knocking down a theory doesn't confirm the opposite conclusion.

paragraph.text: Even if utilitarianism were false, an argument for speciesism would still be needed, and that argument is still missing (A8).

text.bold: 4. The argument attacks the person, not the thesis.

paragraph.text: Discussing what Singer defends on other topics says nothing about whether it's fair to exploit animals (ad hominem).

The Montreal Declaration on Animal Exploitation, from 2022, was signed by more than 500 specialists in moral and political philosophy from some 40 countries, whose work comes from diverse philosophical traditions. A declaration doesn't prove the thesis by itself, but it shows the conclusion doesn't belong to a single school.

text.bold: 6. There are still other non-utilitarian routes.

paragraph.text: The political philosopher Alasdair Cochrane brings several of them together (2010):

text.bold: A contract with species behind the veil.

paragraph.text: Besides Rowlands, Donald VanDeVeer (1979) argues that if being a person is an arbitrary contingency, so is species, which should therefore go behind the veil of ignorance (pp. 61–63).

Katherine Perlo and Barbara Noske describe farmed animals as exploited and alienated, like workers; David Sztybel and Ted Benton extend the principle "to each according to their needs" to animals (pp. 105–112). Cochrane criticizes some of these readings, and the debate continues within the left (K5).
Feminist theorists such as Josephine Donovan and Carol J. Adams start from care and from a critique of domination, not from a utility calculation (pp. 118–120, 130–134).

Proposed by Joel Feinberg (1974) and defended by Cochrane himself, this route uses sentience as the criterion, as utilitarianism does, but protects certain interests with rights that no sum of benefits can override (pp. 47–48, 142–144).
None of these routes depends on accepting utilitarianism, and some were built precisely against it.

(d) The strongest counter-reply: the other theories are weaker on animals

The most serious version grants that other theories consider animals, but says only utilitarianism demands radical change. Rights or contractualist theories would give animals only minimal protections, compatible with some use.

Utilitarianism has serious problems, discussed for over a century, and it's true that
tied the subject to that theory for many people. It's also true that theories differ about what we owe animals in hard cases.
But the central question, whether it's fair to make animals suffer and die for small benefits, gets the same answer from almost all of them.
